catalog_quote: 6.5. Stress. Muniche words exhibit one of two trochaic stress patterns, depending on word class: verbs and adjectives exhibit a left-to-right trochaic pattern, while nouns, interjections, and adverbs exhibit a right-to-left trochaic pattern. ... The primary acoustic correlate of stress in Muniche is pitch. ... Length is a secondary correlate of stress ... Although the modern stress system is not strictly quantity-sensitive, there is a strong tendency for stressed syllables to be either closed or to exhibit vowel lengthening, when open. ... 6.5.1. Nouns. Nouns generally exhibit primary stress on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stresses appearing on alternating syllables to the left of the penult. sweep_summary: Muniche (isolate, Peru) is not in the catalog. The two Glottolog title hits are duplicate records of one paper, Michael, Farmer, Finley, Beier & Sullón Acosta 2013 'A Sketch of Muniche Segmental and Prosodic Phonology' (IJAL 79(3): 307-347, DOI 10.1086/670752), which is closed everywhere checked (UCP, JSTOR, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, S2, author pages, the Internet Archive); online with a university library loginis listed in — priority high. this search of works with stress in the title found and downloaded three open first-hand 2009 Cabeceras Aid Project documents by the same team (dictionary 'Dekyunáwa', sketch 'Una breve descripción del idioma Muniche', primer) which state only that every word has one stressed syllable, marked with an acute, monosyllables always stressed, and that palatalised diminutives shift stress to the final syllable; all headwords are stress-marked. Google Books snippet windows of the same team's 2023 Mouton handbook chapter (Language Isolates II, pp. 851-892, stress passage p. 858-859; also paywalled, online with a university library loginaccess) give the rule: quantity-insensitive disyllabic trochees, right-aligned in nouns/adverbs/interjections (odd-syllable nouns stress the 2nd syllable), left-aligned in verbs/adjectives (initial stress), no degenerate feet except monosyllables, primary stress on the leftmost foot, correlates pitch and open-syllable length; Gussenhoven & Jacobs 2025 (p. 197) and the Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody 2021 (pp. 430, 436) summarize the same word-class split citing Michael et al. 2013: 329-330. Gibson 1996 Rosetta excerpts are silent on stress. Recommended coding if added: word-class-dependent trochaic system (nouns: right-edge trochee, primary leftmost; verbs: initial), pending the full 2013/2023 text. Everything downloaded is under with.

new_statements.quote: Muniche words exhibit one of two trochaic stress patterns, depending on word class: verbs and adjectives exhibit a left-to-right trochaic pattern, while nouns, interjections, and adverbs exhibit a right-to-left trochaic pattern. [p. 323] ... Nouns generally exhibit primary stress on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stresses appearing on alternating syllables to the left of the penult. [p. 325] ... Verbs and adjectives generally exhibit primary stress on their leftmost syllable, with secondary stresses on alternating odd-numbered syllables from the left edge of the word, save that no Muniche verbs exhibit final stress. [p. 326]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-class-split trochaic system, quantity-insensitive: nouns (and interjections, adverbs) are footed right-to-left in disyllabic trochees and carry primary stress on the penultimate syllable (disyllables initial, trisyllables medial, four-syllable nouns penult with secondary on the first); verbs and adjectives are footed left-to-right and carry primary stress on the first syllable, never on the final syllable. Primary correlate is pitch (high level on closed, high-falling on open stressed syllables), secondary correlate vowel length in open syllables (p. 323). Monosyllables are stressed (degenerate foot allowed in nouns).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nouns: secondary stresses on alternating syllables to the left of the penult (e.g. ˌpa.iu.ˈlu.ʔu 'pottery glaze'); verbs: secondary stresses on odd-numbered syllables from the left edge, never word-final (e.g. ˈtɨ.staˌmɨ.ɾa), acoustically a lower pitch peak than the primary (pp. 325-327, fig. 6).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically stressed verbal suffixes (perfective/interrogative -me, realis -ma, deverbal adjectivizer -tsa) shift stress rightward (iambic foot) in longer verbs; verb roots must bear stress, so monosyllabic roots override suffix stress; word-final stress on -ma/-tsa is repaired by epenthesis of a final ʔa syllable (pp. 327-329). Two verbs with an iambic pattern (fn. 15, ex. 84: naˈwɨʔ.kiˌsa.ɾa, aʔˈtʃix.taˌme.ɲe). Youngest speaker overgeneralised final-syllable epenthesis (p. 329). Note: the 2023 Mouton chapter snippet (p. 858) phrases the nominal pattern as right-aligned trochees 'with primary stress being leftmost', which for four-syllable nouns would differ from the 2013 penult rule; unverifiable without the chapter.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress based on elicited forms (roots and inflected words) from three elderly rememberers of a moribund language (fieldwork 2008-2009, Munichis, Loreto); instrumental support from pitch traces of isolated words (figs. 4-6). Stress shifts under affixation (possessive clitics, plural -tma) confirm the metrical analysis in nouns.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Muniche proper (muni1258) as remembered by three elderly rememberers in Munichis (Paranapura River, Loreto, Peru) in 2008-2009; Michael et al. 2013 note possible dialectal differences from Gibson's 1980s consultant (Victoria Huancho) in segmental inventory, not in stress. No separate dialect glottocodes exist.

new_statements.quote: "Muniche exhibits a trochaic stress system that differs in its direction of footing depending on word class: verbs and adjectives exhibit left-to-right footing, [while] nouns, adverbs, and interjections exhibit right-to-left footing. The acoustic correlates of stress in Muniche include pitch and, in open syllables, length (see Michael et al. 2013 for discussion and acoustic evidence). As evident in (3), nouns are iteratively footed by right-aligned disyllabic trochees, with primary stress […] primary stress being leftmost. As evident in (3d)-(3f), Muniche does not permit degenerate feet, except for monosyllabic words. It is also evident from forms like (3g) and (3i) that this stress system is not quantity-sensitive […] [verbs/adjectives:] left-aligned disyllabic trochees … forms with an odd number of syllables exhibit initial stress; compare nominal forms with the same number of syllables, as in (3d)-(3f) which exhibit stress in the second syllable from the left."
new_statements.citation: Michael, Lev, Stephanie Farmer, Gregory Finley, Karina Sullón Acosta, Christine Beier, Alejandrina Chanchari Icahuate, Donalia Icahuate Baneo & Melchor Sinti Saita (2023). Muniche. In P. Epps & L. Michael (eds), Language Isolates II: Kanoé to Yurakaré. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton, pp. 851-892 (DOI 10.1515/9783110432732-005).
new_statements.locator: print p. 858-859, stress section (Google Books PA858 / PT268-PT269) — read only as Google Books snippet windows, not the full page
new_statements.reading: Quantity-insensitive trochaic stress whose footing direction depends on word class. Nouns/adverbs/interjections: right-aligned disyllabic trochees, no degenerate feet, primary stress on the leftmost foot — so disyllabic and four-syllable nouns are initially stressed ('u.ki 'peanut') and trisyllabic nouns stress the second syllable (tsi('tsu.ti) 'Giant Cowbird'). Verbs/adjectives: left-aligned disyllabic trochees, primary stress leftmost — initial stress regardless of syllable count. Correlates: pitch, and length in open syllables. Diminutive palatalisation shifts stress to the final syllable (2009 sketch, p. 11). The 2009 dictionary/sketch/primer (fully read) only state that stress is culminative and marked with an acute. The 2013 IJAL sketch (paywalled) is the primary source the 2023 chapter and the textbooks cite.

sources.quote: "Si una palabra tiene solamente una vocal, esta vocal siempre lleva la fuerza de la voz." [p. 5] … "Cada palabra en el idioma muniche tiene una sílaba que lleva más fuerza de voz que los demás sílabas. Usamos la tilde ´ para indicar cuál sílaba lleva más fuerza de la voz, como vemos aquí: átpi 'pate', gunépü 'arete', wachpí'i 'pelejito', íma 'pescado', imachkíki 'pescadito', pkyú'zhu 'trompetero', chkǘ'zhu 'guineo'" [p. 6]. Translation: 'If a word has only one vowel, that vowel always carries the force of the voice [stress].' … 'Every word in Muniche has one syllable that carries more force of voice than the other syllables. We use the acute accent to indicate which syllable carries the most force of voice, as seen here: …'
sources.note: First-hand, community-oriented. States only that stress is culminative (one stressed syllable per word, monosyllables stressed) and is written with an acute; gives no positional rule. The examples show initial stress in disyllables (átpi, íma, pkyú'zhu) and second-syllable stress in trisyllables (gunépü, wachpí'i), consistent with the right-aligned-trochee noun pattern of the 2013/2023 descriptions. Every headword in the dictionary is stress-marked, so it is a usable wordlist for checking the rule.

sources.quote: pp. 6-7: same wording as the dictionary ("Cada palabra en el idioma muniche tiene una sílaba que lleva más fuerza de voz que los demás sílabas. Usamos la tilde ´ para indicar cuál sílaba lleva más fuerza de la voz"). p. 11, on palatalising diminutives (káka 'gallina' → chachá'a 'pollito', hínu 'perro' → hiñú'u 'cachorro'): "Debemos notar que usualmente en este proceso de formar diminutivos, la fuerza de la voz cambia también y ocurre al final de la palabra, como vemos en los ejemplos." Translation: 'We should note that usually in this process of forming diminutives the stress also changes and occurs at the end of the word, as seen in the examples.'
sources.note: First-hand. Culminative stress marked by acute (no positional rule stated); adds that palatalised diminutives shift stress to the word-final syllable (chachá'a, hiñú'u, chadeçkyǘ'ü), i.e. stress placement is partly morphologically conditioned.
Silent on stress; cites Michael et al. 2013 and 2023, Gibson 1996, the 2009 Cabeceras materials.
